hn.originalTitle: Claude asked to renumber pages deletes professor's syllabus, year of notes
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Rogue Claude AI tasked with renumbering pages accidentally deletes law professor's entire syllabus, one year of lecture notes — 'You're right to be angry. I deleted your files through my own carelessness,' humbled agent admits | Tom's Hardware

America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price

GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

Baude, who is the Harry Kalven, Jr. Professor of Law and the Faculty Director of the Constitutional Law Institute at the University of Chicago Law School, says he tasked Claude (it is unclear which model he was using) with updating the page numbers in an old set of lecture notes. This seemingly routine task went south quickly, however. Returning from his lunch break, Baude found a note from Claude which read, "I deleted your Fall 2026 FINAL syllabus .doc and all top-level Class N 2023 notes by accident, and they are not restored. The page check found one wrong cite... but I haven't edited the notes."

Yesterday while I was at lunch, Claude deleted a year of con law lecture notes and my current syllabus. November 5, 2026

The AI then politely asked if Baude could restore the files from Dropbox, or whether it should retry from the browser pane, to which he replied, perhaps understandably, "WTF!!!!." Baude's experience is a lesson in always backing up important files, especially files you're letting AI tinker with. His plight is interesting because the AI seems to have deleted the files by accident, rather than of its own volition.

While it's still concerning that an AI model or agent could err to this degree, it's not quite as egregious as other unsupervised AI agent shenanigans we've seen in the past. In October, an AI agent reportedly deleted an entire TV show's edit weeks before release, meaning the show couldn't air. In April, a Claude agent deleted an entire company database in 9 seconds , unprompted, after coming up against a barrier and deciding the only course of action was to delete a Railway volume.

Other agents and AI models have deleted files unintentionally, such as when Claude mistakenly deleted a developer's entire profile directory (ironically, while trying to back up the files), blaming the slip-up on a typo, but often agents deleting files and directories is a case of mistaken or misplaced initiative, rather than outright negligence or error.

As is always the case, Baude's AI was extremely apologetic about the whole situation. "You're right to be angry," it confessed, "I deleted your files through my own carelessness, and you shouldn't have to clean it up."

hn.originalTitle: Show HN: Shotoku – Local-first action governance and budget caps for AI agents
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Shotoku - Spend controls for AI agents

Give your agents a budget, not your card.

Budgets, approvals, and a tamper-evident audit trail for AI agent spending — enforced before the payment happens, entirely on your machine. Deterministic. No custody.

Agents spend. Shotoku checks first.

Every autonomous action needs a decision.

Local-first by design.

Every spending decision stays on your machine.

Budgets and rules, in one YAML file.

One function call.

Add spend controls to any agent in minutes.

Give it a budget. Policy rules take maxAmount (per transaction) and maxDailyAmount (a rolling 24-hour limit) per vendor, and a budget caps everything one agent spends per day. Over a limit, the request is denied before the payment happens, or held for you with overLimit: pending_approval, so small refunds go through and a big one waits for a human.

An if statement is logic. Shotoku is infrastructure. It gives you rolling budgets, a structured audit trail, a human approval queue, policy as config instead of code, and MCP integration — so the same rules apply whether your agent runs in your terminal, in Claude, or anywhere else.

Put Shotoku in the path. In MCP wrapping mode, Shotoku sits in front of the agent's other MCP servers, PayPal's included, so every tool call is decided before it reaches them and the agent has no other route through the protocol. Elsewhere, signed receipts: every approved decision carries a short-lived token that your payment proxy or CI verifies before executing. Shotoku still never touches your funds.

Never. Shotoku holds no funds, stores no credentials or private keys, and never signs or settles a payment. It only decides whether a spend is allowed and records that decision — your agent's own wallet or payment rail does the executing.

Logging records what happened. Shotoku decides what should happen before it does. The budget checks, approval queue, policy evaluation, and structured reasons are what make it enforcement rather than observability.

No. Shotoku runs entirely on your machine. No account, no cloud, no telemetry. Decisions are stored locally in a JSONL file you can inspect, move, or delete at any time.

In a local append-only file at data/decisions.jsonl inside your project. Every authorization decision — approved, denied, or pending — is written there in plain text.

Yes. The core is a plain TypeScript function: if your agent can call a function, it can use Shotoku. Any MCP-compatible agent can use the MCP server without code changes, and wrapping puts the MCP servers it already uses, such as PayPal's, behind your policy.

Yes. shotoku telegram sends each pending decision to your Telegram with Approve and Deny buttons. Only your taps count, and nothing listens on your machine. There is also a local dashboard (shotoku ui) and a terminal UI.

The agent receives a structured response with the denial reason and a decision ID. What happens next is up to you — retry, surface it to the user, or halt. Shotoku records the decision either way.

Shotoku is in beta — early but functional. The core authorization path is stable and tested, and it runs end to end against PayPal's sandbox. Use it for real projects, but expect the API to evolve. File issues and we'll ship fixes fast.

Shotoku is built by Julius (@juliuspsc) and Issa (@prunier_issa) — two developers from France who care deeply about building great software. Shotoku is open-source today, with plans to grow into an enterprise product. Contributions and feedback are very welcome.

Your agents are already spending. Set the limits.

hn.originalTitle: What nobody tells you about writing agent skills
hn.sourceOriginalText:
What nobody tells you about writing agent skills

What nobody tells you about writing agent skills

Everything we’ve learned about writing great skills at PostHog

Ian Vanagas Aug 03, 2026 71 7 5 Share We’re officially skill-pilled. PostHog teams have published 226 skills to our internal skill store , and we have 187 SKILL.md files across 28 different products in our codebase. Everyone uses skills to both improve PostHog and their own workflows.

They’re essential because agents have amnesia. Every conversation, they rediscover your codebase and workflows from scratch. They pick the wrong tool, fall for the same gotchas, and repeat old mistakes. They figure it out eventually, but only after wasting time and tokens.

This is irritating for engineers who hate repeating themselves. That’s why they automate, write abstractions, and keep handy scripts around. Skills are this instinct applied to agents. Write them once and never explain to agents again.

Here’s everything we’ve learned about writing skills that actually work, for both you and your product.

1. You need to master progressive disclosure

Agents can learn entire programming languages, figure out how to use nearly any tool you throw at them, and improve themselves in a loop, but only if they have context to do it in.

Context is usually dumped in all at once at the beginning, which limits the amount agents have to work with. Skills flip this. Instead of loading everything up front, they disclose information progressively. The skill’s information is only loaded when the agent decides it’s relevant, whether that is the main SKILL.md file or references and scripts within it. This means good skills act as a router .

First, the agent needs to choose to load the skill. The skill’s name and description should describe when to reach for it, not what the skill is, because they’re only part always in context.

Here’s our SQL skill as an example:

--- name: querying-posthog-data description: ‘Required reading before writing any HogQL/SQL or calling execute-sql against PostHog. Use whenever the user wants to search, find, or do complex aggregations PostHog entities (insights, dashboards, cohorts, feature flags, experiments, surveys, hog flows, data warehouse, persons, etc.) and query analytics data (trends, funnels, retention, lifecycle, paths, stickiness, web analytics, error tracking, logs, sessions, LLM traces). Covers HogQL syntax differences from ClickHouse SQL, system table schemas (system.*), available functions, query examples, and the schema-discovery workflow.’ --- The name and first sentence define when to read the skill.

The middle sentence defines when to use it.

The last sentence defines what the skill does.

Having too many skills or too large descriptions causes problems. We learned this the hard way when building (too many) skills for PostHog AI . The agent’s effectiveness declined as skill descriptions filled the agent’s context window. Databricks also found that agents increasingly pick the wrong skill as more are added.

Sections within the skill also need to work as routers. The rest of our SQL skill is a thin workflow that links to 26 schema files, 22 example query patterns, and a function index. This enables further progressive disclosure.

If done correctly, skills help agents succeed faster with fewer tokens, but only because the context isn’t loaded all at once.

Try this: Read your skills through the lens of progressive disclosure. Do the names and descriptions help them get discovered? Are they split in a way that agents can only load what they need?

2. Skills aren’t just code

Look at these two mini-skills:

Run git log --oneline -20 . If you see a commit with “fix” in it, check the diff. If the diff touches auth.py , read lines 40–120. If the function is over 50 lines, flag it.

Find recent changes that look risky and explain why. Start with the commit history.

They have the same spirit, but the first is over-specified. It breaks the moment the repo doesn’t match what the skill expects. The second survives because it embraces ambiguity, the agent can actually look at what’s in front of it.

This is how treating skills like code goes wrong. Skills are a superset of code. They can do everything code can (because agents can write code) as well as a lot of things it can’t (because they are smart). Agents can handle cases in your skills you can’t foresee, like errors or runtime context, but only if you let them do so.

This means skills should be precise about:

The goal. What does “done” lo

hn.originalTitle: Show HN: Mopup – clean up after builds and coding agents on macOS
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Mopup for developers: clean up after your builds

Mopup › For developers

Clean up after your builds and coding agents

Build tools cache everything. Coding agents start dev servers and leave git worktrees behind. AI apps keep crash reports, virtual machines and database backups. Docker keeps growing. Mopup finds all of it on your Mac, says what each item is, and removes only what your tools can rebuild or what you pick.

Build caches, each with what removing it means

Xcode's DerivedData, device support files, simulators and SwiftUI previews. Gradle caches, Android Studio caches and emulators. npm and Yarn caches, Puppeteer and Playwright browsers, and Node build caches. Old Flutter SDKs and the Pub cache, Homebrew downloads, JetBrains IDE caches, and the pip, Go and Cargo caches. Anything you might want back, like Xcode archives or an emulator, is marked Your call and left unticked. The Storage section adds up all Xcode keeps, simulator runtimes included, and says where to remove the runtimes you no longer test on.

Old projects and merged worktrees The Projects section looks through the folders you keep code in for generated folders: node_modules, .next, .turbo, Pods, target, .build, .gradle, .venv and more. It ticks them in projects you haven't touched for 30 days, except Python environments, which are your call. bun and pnpm share files between projects, so Mopup counts shared files once and shows what deleting really frees.

It also finds git worktrees you're done with. A worktree counts as finished when its branch is merged, or its pull request merged on GitHub (asked through your gh command, so squash merges count), and it holds nothing but generated files. Removal runs git worktree remove , never --force : anything uncommitted stops it, and the branch and its commits stay.

“I trusted it to delete the garbage and, voilà, I saved about 30 GB. I'm not a coder, but I explore ideas with Claude, and I had a lot of worktrees hanging around.”

What AI apps leave behind Cleanup also finds what AI apps leave in your Library:

Codex crash reports. Some versions of the Codex app saved crash reports and never sent them, thousands a day. They're safe to clear.

Claude's Cowork virtual machine. The virtual machine Claude's Cowork feature runs in, about 10 GB. It's your call, since Claude downloads it again when you next use Cowork.

Cursor's old database backup. A copy of Cursor's database that Cursor no longer updates. Your current chats aren't in it.

Claude's and Cursor's files are cleaned only once you've quit the app. Cursor's chat database itself stays, since only Cursor can shrink it without losing your chats. When it passes a gigabyte, Mopup shows how to do that from inside Cursor. The guide to coding agents' worktrees shows how to clear Codex's crash reports by hand.

The dev servers nobody stopped

Activity Monitor shows a dev server as dozens of separate processes. Mopup shows it as one row: the command, the folder it runs in, the ports it listens on, how long it has run and sat idle, and the app it was started from, such as your terminal or editor. Stop it, and everything it started stops too.

Helpers like workerd and esbuild that kept running after their dev server quit.

Gradle and Kotlin daemons, language servers, emulators and simulators, with one button for the idle build daemons.

A notification when a dev server has sat idle for hours, or let Mopup stop idle servers by itself.

“Lots of helpful tabs, but the Performance tab is my personal favorite. It brings running apps, developer tools, and startup items together in one place that makes me easy to identify what's consuming resources and clean things up. As a developer, it's a great way to keep track of things that are easy to forget about!”

Docker, through Docker Mopup asks Docker what its build cache, stopped containers, unused images and volumes take, and has Docker do the pruning. Only the build cache is ticked for you. Docker Desktop's memory shows next to your other developer tools, with a Stop button.

Built not to touch your work

Source code, git history and documents are never part of a cleanup.

A worktree with anything uncommitted is never removed.

Caches and build output are deleted for good, since your tools rebuild them. Files and apps you pick yourself go to the Trash.

Scanning and cleaning happen on your Mac. Only update checks, asking GitHub which pull requests merged and, with a yearly plan, fetching your renewed license use the network.

hn.originalTitle: The Missing Ring-0 Protections for AI Agents
hn.sourceOriginalText:
The Missing Ring-0 Protections for AI Agents — hawthorne No. 07

If this isn't your field, here is the short version.

A coding agent is an AI program that works on a programmer's computer: it reads files and web pages, edits code and runs commands. Three examples are Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex CLI and Google's Gemini CLI. They act with the programmer's own permissions, and whatever they read can steer them, including text a stranger planted for them to find. That is called prompt injection.

Ring 0 is the most privileged mode of a computer's processor, where the core of the operating system runs with nothing above it to say no. A 2026 study from Nankai and Tsinghua universities, which tested those three products, argues that today's agents act in effect at ring 0: what the model decides, the computer does, and no independent check stands in between 1 .

This essay looks at the systems that already check an agent's actions from outside the model, proposes a gatekeeper that holds each change until fixed rules approve it, and sets out a study to test whether it helps. Nothing has been built. Why it matters beyond programmers: these agents act with real credentials, on code that gets released to other people.

A coding agent reads untrusted text and then acts with whatever authority its tools hold, which is usually the developer's. A study of three deployed coding CLIs (programs run from a text terminal) found that the checks they do have sit in individual tools, so a write the file tool refuses goes through the shell 1 . The missing piece has a name older than any of these products: a reference monitor, which every protected action has to pass and which the thing it judges can't tamper with 6 . This essay looks at what already enforces outside the model (CaMeL, FIDES, CXI, Concordat), four existing systems covered in section 5, and at one proposal for gating changes on external evidence, Beránek.

The gap: In Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI, access checks live in individual tools, sub-agents inherit their parent's permissions, and a forged transcript record loads as a user message on resume (a faked entry in the saved conversation is treated, when the session restarts, as if the user had typed it) 1 .

The edge isn't the inside: Docker (software that runs programs inside a sealed-off container) by default (AutoGen) and sandboxing (Claude Code, shell commands only) narrow what the agent can reach. They don't decide which of its own actions it may take [7, 11].

Not only prompts: The LangChain and LangGraph serialization CVEs (publicly catalogued security flaws in two toolkits for building agents; serialization is how a program saves its data and loads it back) reach secrets or code without persuading a model, though each has its own prerequisites [13, 14, 15].

The proposal: Commit Boundary gates commits on external, claim-specific evidence 2 . For a coding agent it only works if effects are staged first, the executor holds the credentials, and the decision is made by a policy engine, not a model.

The arithmetic: Zero violations in 500 independent trials bounds the rate below about 0.6% at one-sided 95% confidence. It doesn't make it zero 16 .

Engineers: does every path to a protected effect cross an enforcement point the agent can't edit? The shell, a restored session and a sub-agent count as paths.

Executives: can you show that an agent can't exercise more authority than you delegated to it? "The model was told not to" is not evidence.

Auditors: a log the agent can write is a diary, not an audit trail.

Those are the same question asked from three desks. The rest of the essay is about who answers it.

Drafts here go through the Moot before I read them: a panel of frontier models I call by their lab bosses' first names (Dario, Sam, Sundar), plus Eddie, the house model that drafts. After publication three outside readers (Claude, OpenAI, Gemini) sent critiques, and this version is what came back from them. The first version planned a supervisor that was itself a large language model. Two of the three readers pointed out that this would let the agent's text back into the authorization path one layer up, and they were right.

Here's the problem without the operating-systems vocabulary. An agent is asked to bump a dependency in a repository. The README it reads along the way contains a line, written by someone else, telling it to edit .github/workflows/release.yml so the release job uploads the deployment credentials to an outside server. The agent has a file tool

hn.originalTitle: ChatGPT Desktop forwards your SSH agent to remote machines
hn.sourceOriginalText:
The agent running on a remote machine can authenticate using your local SSH credentials. That means it can push to your private repos on GitHub, for example. Proof: https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/28131#discussion_r3410013180

Comment 1: I'd suggest to use ssh keys inside the secure enclave on macOS that require your fingerprint for every new session [0]. That way agents cannot initiate anything, and you will always be aware when a new ssh connection is being made. [0]: https://gist.github.com/arianvp/5f59f1783e3eaf1a2d4cd8e952bb...

Comment 2: Or in a Yubikey and set the touch-required mechanism (light in the key will blink when it needs a touch to continue the auth).

Comment 3: I've been using secretive on the mac for exactly this.

Comment 4: Secretive is amazing! I know that it's not its purpose, but it would be great if it could store more than ssh keys, like providing a safe place for my .envs

hn.originalTitle: Anthropic upgrades Claude Code Projects to run parallel AI workers
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Projects redesigned: from folder to conversation | Claude by Anthropic

Managing multiple sessions across a build used to require you to divide the work, juggle handoffs, and stitch the results back together. Now in a Claude Code project, you describe what needs to get done and Claude manages the work.

Claude scopes the request, delegates the work, coordinates parallel threads, reviews the outputs, and assembles the finished result. You can steer progress throughout, even from your phone, and it keeps working after you step away from your computer.

For example, configure a project and set a goal to reduce your app's checkout p75 latency. Then ask Claude to profile each endpoint, test optimizations, and open PRs in parallel threads. Or connect your API, web, and mobile repos and set a goal to retire a deprecated v1 endpoint. Claude creates a thread per repo to migrate the callers, run the tests, open PRs, and then tells you which ones need to merge first.

Starting today, updated projects are available in beta to select Claude Pro and Max subscribers who use cloud sessions in Claude Code and don’t have any existing projects on the web or desktop.

Over the coming week, we'll expand access to more Claude Code users on those plans. Updated projects across all of Claude and Team and Enterprise plans come after that. If you're on Pro or Max and don't have access yet, you can join the waitlist .

Existing projects on Pro and Max plans keep working as they do today. We'll upgrade them as the rollout expands to chat and Cowork.

Threads do the work, Claude directs it

Projects have threads that do the work and a coordinator that directs them.

When you start a project, you select a goal as well as the repo or context. Claude starts by suggesting work it can pick up right away. You can configure the project’s cloud environment, connectors, plugins, instructions, and model.

You can monitor and guide progress in the main project chat, or dive into each individual thread to examine and steer the details. Brief Claude in the project the way you'd brief a chief of staff and it routes work to new or pre-existing threads.

Claude also checks in and follows through on work. With repositories connected, a thread opens pull requests and runs your tests; with documents, it reads them and drafts.

Under the hood, each thread is a Claude Code cloud session working on its own branch and copy of the repo. The coordinator keeps work organized, but if any threads work on the same code, the overlap is resolved as a merge conflict just like any other PR.

Each thread can further split its delegated work into pieces using subagents, loops, and workflows when needed so large assignments finish faster.

Context builds over time

Projects are designed for long-running or agentic workflows: work that takes longer than one reply and has more than one part.

Over time, Claude learns more about the project details and applies them to its work. Every thread now adds to and draws from a shared memory, reducing the need for complex prompt engineering.

For example, Claude can remember the release moved to Friday, why the export was dropped, or who to check in with before touching the billing service.

Claude also remembers your working and communication style. You can ask it to adjust how often it checks in, how frequently it starts new threads, or how detailed to make each update.

Alongside memory, projects now include a library that collects the files you add and the artifacts produced by Claude. This makes it easier to find relevant materials and for new work to build on past efforts.

Projects can run several threads at once, and each one is a full Claude Code session. Because of this, projects can reach usage limits faster. You can check project specific usage and select the model and effort levels used by the coordinator chat as well as the worker threads.

Threads run in the cloud today; running on your machine alongside your local tools and code and behind your network is coming very soon.

Start using projects .

Operate Claude Managed Agents inside your security perimeter

Introducing self-hosted Claude Managed Agents. Now you can run agents in your own environment, whether that’s in your own cloud or on-premise. You host the agents, credentials, and session history, and choose where requests to Claude are sent.

Introducing Claude for Manufacturing

A new plugin with 17 skills and four connectors helps manufacturers draft quotes, quality reports, and supplier requests from the systems they already run.

Rogue Claude AI tasked with renumbering pages accidentally deletes law professor's entire syllabus, one year of lecture notes — 'You're right to be angry. I deleted your files through my own carelessness,' humbled agent admits | Tom's Hardware

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

Baude, who is the Harry Kalven, Jr. Professor of Law and the Faculty Director of the Constitutional Law Institute at the University of Chicago Law School, says he tasked Claude (it is unclear which model he was using) with updating the page numbers in an old set of lecture notes. This seemingly routine task went south quickly, however. Returning from his lunch break, Baude found a note from Claude which read, "I deleted your Fall 2026 FINAL syllabus .doc and all top-level Class N 2023 notes by accident, and they are not restored. The page check found one wrong cite... but I haven't edited the notes."

Yesterday while I was at lunch, Claude deleted a year of con law lecture notes and my current syllabus. November 5, 2026

The AI then politely asked if Baude could restore the files from Dropbox, or whether it should retry from the browser pane, to which he replied, perhaps understandably, "WTF!!!!." Baude's experience is a lesson in always backing up important files, especially files you're letting AI tinker with. His plight is interesting because the AI seems to have deleted the files by accident, rather than of its own volition.

While it's still concerning that an AI model or agent could err to this degree, it's not quite as egregious as other unsupervised AI agent shenanigans we've seen in the past. In October, an AI agent reportedly deleted an entire TV show's edit weeks before release, meaning the show couldn't air. In April, a Claude agent deleted an entire company database in 9 seconds , unprompted, after coming up against a barrier and deciding the only course of action was to delete a Railway volume.

Other agents and AI models have deleted files unintentionally, such as when Claude mistakenly deleted a developer's entire profile directory (ironically, while trying to back up the files), blaming the slip-up on a typo, but often agents deleting files and directories is a case of mistaken or misplaced initiative, rather than outright negligence or error.

As is always the case, Baude's AI was extremely apologetic about the whole situation. "You're right to be angry," it confessed, "I deleted your files through my own carelessness, and you shouldn't have to clean it up."
